lesson.title: A Pamphlet That Changed a Continent: Common Sense
lesson.summary: Published in January 1776, Thomas Paine's plainly written pamphlet Common Sense argued forcefully for independence and helped turn a colonial rebellion into a movement for a new nation.
lesson.body:
By late 1775, the Second Continental Congress had created an army, fought battles, and even sent the Olive Branch Petition to King George III, yet most colonists still described themselves as loyal subjects seeking redress rather than revolutionaries seeking a new country. Independence remained a radical, almost unspeakable idea for many, something raised only in private conversation. Into this uncertain moment came a pamphlet that pushed public opinion further and faster than any single document had before.

Thomas Paine was a relatively recent arrival in America, having emigrated from England in 1774 with the encouragement of Benjamin Franklin, whom he had met in London. Paine worked briefly as a magazine editor in Philadelphia before turning his full attention to the political crisis unfolding around him. In January 1776 he published Common Sense anonymously, since its arguments were bold enough that an unpopular reception might have brought serious consequences to its author, and the pamphlet was at first widely attributed to other, better known writers.

What set Common Sense apart was not just its argument but its style. Paine wrote in direct, plain language meant for ordinary readers rather than the formal, classically inflected prose common among educated elites of the era. He attacked the very idea of hereditary monarchy as irrational, ridiculing the notion that one family should rule simply by birth regardless of ability, and he argued that continued loyalty to a distant king made no practical sense for a growing, self sufficient continent capable of governing itself. Paine insisted that reconciliation with Britain was no longer realistic and that only complete independence would secure colonists' rights and future prosperity.

The pamphlet was an immediate sensation. It sold well over one hundred thousand copies within its first few months, an extraordinary number for a colonial population of roughly two and a half million people, and it was read aloud in taverns, printed in newspapers, and passed hand to hand across the colonies. George Washington himself noted the shift in sentiment it seemed to produce among soldiers and civilians alike as copies circulated through army camps.

Common Sense did not single handedly cause the movement for independence, which had been building since the Intolerable Acts and the fighting at Lexington and Concord, but it gave that movement a vocabulary and an argument that ordinary people could repeat and believe without needing a formal education. By making independence sound not just possible but obviously reasonable, Paine helped clear the political ground for the Second Continental Congress to move, within just a few months, toward the Declaration of Independence.

Paine structured the pamphlet in four parts, moving from a general critique of government and monarchy to a direct argument for why the American colonies specifically should separate from Britain immediately rather than wait for a more convenient moment. He donated the proceeds from the pamphlet to the Continental Army, a gesture that reinforced his claim to be arguing from principle rather than personal ambition.
